newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - May 30.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - May 30.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Five months ago, Rupert Murdoch said in Tokyo that the first nine months of the Federal Government had seen a "pretty bad" pace of reform. His comments coincided with a meeting of the Advisory Committee on Policy, chaired by Prime Minister John Howard. As media policy was being discussed that day, Murdoch has been on the backfoot ever since. Page 1.

About 300 staff of Citibank Australia will be retrenched by the end of the year in a drastic move responding to the margin squeeze in Australian banking. The cuts of about a sixth of the company's workforce will be focused on the bank's mortgage, deposit and credit card operations. Page 1.

Yesterday's tabling of House of Representatives members' travel claims in Parliament showed Labor Party MPs over the past few years have claimed for more travel allowances than the Coalition. The tabling of claims follows the tabling of a similar document for Senate members, with both documents aimed at restoring the image of MPs. Page 3.

A review of Australia's national energy policies by the International Energy Agency has found that there is potential for the nation to improve its energy efficiency, a finding that could be used as ammunition for opponents against Australia's stance for a special greenhouse gas deal. Page 5.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Justice Hedigan of the Supreme Court yesterday overturned the Australian Football League's nine-week suspension of Carlton's Greg Williams on the charge of unduly interfering with an umpire. The decision indicates a new ball game, that Williams' manager Peter Jess proclaimed had changed the face of sport. Page 1.

A Coalition meeting has indicated the Federal Government will further cut tariff protection for Australian car makers, but the cuts will be less than those recommended by the Productivity Commission. While it appeared there would be a backbench revolt against the lowering of tariffs, it was made clear yesterday that further changes would be accepted. Page 1.

Official Department of Administrative Services figures tabled in Parliament yesterday show nine former Keating ministers have been forced to repay the Federal Government almost A$6,000 in allowances after falsely claiming thousands of dollars in travel expenses. Page 3.

The Independent Commission Against Corruption heard yesterday that New South Wales Aboriginal land councils wasted millions of dollars on alcohol and "obscure" financial investments instead of funding housing projects. The revelations came on the first day of a six-week inquiry into corruption in five of the state's land councils that follow an 18-month investigation into over 200 complaints. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

New South Wales Premier Bob Carr said yesterday the decision on the A$22 billion sale of the state's electricity industry would not be taken to the Australian Labor Party state conference in October, effectively leaving unions and the left wing without their main forum to defeat the sale. Page 1.

Alleged pedophile Philip Bell, 62, will arrive in Sydney tonight after being extradited from South Africa and being on the run from New South Wales police for the past 14 months. Bell will appear in the Central Court on Saturday to face 200 charges of sexual offences against boys. Page 1.

Under the 2000 Games Homestay programme, Sydney residents could enjoy takings of up to four times the normal rent on their home from visitors. Prices will depend on the grading of the property, which will range from standard, superior, or luxurious, with house normally fetching A$350 a week in rent expected to get around A$1400 a week during the Olympics. Page 1.

The Federal Government last night gained the vote of Independent Senator Brian Harradine to both end Commonwealth controls on minerals exports and block an attempt to retain ceilings on native forest exports of whole logs and woodchips. Harradine last year voted against such moves, leading Greens Senator Bob Brown to question his motives. Page 3.
THE AGE

Melbourne-based Australian Independent Newspapers says it would be interested in purchasing a significant part of the Fairfax newspaper group, or a part of one of its titles. The move by the group, which made an unsuccessful bid for Fairfax in 1991, complicates the situation for Kerry Packer, who wishes to takeover Fairfax. Page 1.

Victorian Attorney-General Jan Wade has sought leave to intervene in a Supreme Court hearing next month that will decide the fate of Legislative Council Liberal MP Bruce Atkinson, who is fighting an Opposition bid to have him thrown out of Parliament. The Opposition said Wade's support for Atkinson was a desperate use of government resources and taxpayers' money. Page 1.

Prime Minister John Howard is reluctant to preside over the Japanese Sumo Association's historic Australian tour which is a key part of celebrations in Australia and Japan marking the 100-year anniversary of diplomatic relations. Some observers believe the refusal is tantamount to an official snub. Page 1.

Human Rights and Equal Opportunity president Sir Ronald Wilson said yesterday in Canberra, where he was handing over the commission's report on the separation of Aboriginal children from their parents, that a government refusal to pay compensation to the stolen generations of Aborigines could lead to a flood of compensation cases in Australia's courts. Page 1.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
